blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews JaVerT, a JavaScript Verification Toolchain designed to verify functional correctness properties of JavaScript programs through annotations like pre-/post-conditions and loop invariants. The tool addresses JavaScript's dynamic behaviors (e.g., extensible objects, dynamic property access) by first compiling JavaScript to an intermediate language (JSIL) via a logic-preserving compiler (JS-2-JSIL). JaVerT uses JS Logic, a separation logic with heap models and predicates for JavaScript-specific structures (e.g., prototype chains, closures), to write specifications that abstract heap details for developers. The verification process relies on JSIL Verify, a semi-automatic tool combining symbolic execution and an entailment engine (using Z3 SMT solver) to check Hoare triples. The authors also axiomatize JavaScript internal functions (e.g., GetValue, PutValue) to enable reasoning about core language behaviors. JaVerT targets critical JavaScript code like Node.js libraries, aiming to ensure correctness in complex dynamic scenarios.
paper_abstract: Having high-quality and reliable software is an increasingly stringent requirement for most organisations. While traditional static program analysis techniques, such as symbolic execution and formal verification, can help produce error-free software, their successful application to large, rapidly-changing codebases has been limited. In response to this, recent years have seen the development of a number of tools that specifically target their analysis at real-world projects. At Facebook, the Infer tool has been successfully deployed to find lightweight bugs in codebases spanning millions of lines of code, by leveraging various continuous reasoning techniques. This project extends Gillian, a multi-language platform for symbolic analysis developed in the Verified Software group at Imperial, with continuous reasoning foundations that substantially advance its applicability to real-world projects. In particular, we have: extended its instantiations for C and JavaScript in order to allow them to analyse multi-file projects; and incorporated a mechanism for reusing previously-stored results in order to focus analysis on only the fragments of the source program that have changed. Finally, by analysing two real-world JavaScript and C projects, we have demonstrated the significant improvement in the usability of Gillian by a general developer, as well as the correctness of our implementation.
